title: Standard form
summary: [[standard-form|Standard form]] writes a very large or very small number as a number from $1$ to just under $10$, times a power of $10$. You'll convert numbers into and out of standard form, and multiply, divide, add and subtract with them.

goals.text: Say whether a number is in standard form, $A \times 10^{n}$ with $1 \le A < 10$.
Write ordinary numbers in standard form, and standard form as ordinary numbers.
Multiply, divide, add and subtract numbers in standard form, by hand and with a calculator.

synonyms: very large and very small numbers

before.prompt: Write $10^{4} \times 10^{5}$ as a single power of $10$.
before.hint: When you multiply powers of the same number, what happens to the indices?
before.explain: Multiplying powers of $10$ adds the indices: $4 + 5 = 9$. Revise it in {{lesson:1.7}}.
$10^{-2} = \frac{1}{100} = 0.01$. A negative power is never a negative number here. Revise it in {{lesson:1.7}}.

blocks.text: Numbers like $93\,000\,000\,000$ or $0.000\,000\,52$ are hard to read and easy to copy wrongly. Powers of $10$ write them neatly.

The [[index|index]] of $10$ counts places: $10^{3} = 1000$, $10^{1} = 10$, $10^{0} = 1$, $10^{-1} = 0.1$ and $10^{-3} = 0.001$. A [[negative-index|negative index]] means divide by $10$ that many times.

blocks.statement: A number is in [[standard-form|standard form]] when it is written as $A \times 10^{n}$, where $1 \le A < 10$ and $n$ is an integer (positive, negative or zero).
blocks.plain: Exactly one non-zero digit before the decimal point, times a power of $10$.

blocks.text: So $4.07 \times 10^{5}$ is in standard form. $40.7 \times 10^{4}$ is not, because $40.7$ is $10$ or more. $0.407 \times 10^{6}$ is not, because $0.407$ is less than $1$. All three equal $407\,000$.
To turn standard form into an ordinary number, multiply by the power of $10$. A positive $n$ moves the decimal point $n$ places right. A negative power such as $10^{-4}$ moves it $4$ places left.

blocks.question: Write $7.36 \times 10^{5}$ as an ordinary number.
steps: $10^{5}$ means multiply by $10$ five times, so move the decimal point $5$ places right.
$7.36$ has two digits after the point. Fill the other $3$ places with zeros: $736\,000$.
Check: a positive power should give a number of $10$ or more. It does.

blocks.question: Write $2.9 \times 10^{-4}$ as an ordinary number.
steps: $10^{-4}$ means divide by $10$ four times, so move the decimal point $4$ places left.
Fill the gaps with zeros: $2.9$ becomes $0.00029$.
Check: a negative power should give a number less than $1$. It does.

blocks.hint: Move the decimal point $3$ places left.
blocks.explain: Three places left from $8.4$: $0.84$, $0.084$, $0.0084$. $8400$ is what $10^{3}$ would give.

blocks.prompt: Which of these is $0.00508$ written in standard form?
blocks.hint: There must be exactly one non-zero digit before the decimal point.
blocks.explain: $50.8$ is too big and $0.508$ too small to be $A$. $5.08 \times 10^{3}$ is $5080$, not $0.00508$.

sections.heading: Writing a number in standard form

blocks.text: 1. Put the decimal point just after the first non-zero digit. This gives $A$.
2. Count how many places the point moved. That count is the size of $n$.
3. For a positive number: if it is $10$ or more, $n$ is positive. If it is less than $1$, $n$ is negative. If it is at least $1$ but less than $10$, $n = 0$.

blocks.question: Write $58\,400\,000$ in [[standard-form|standard form]].
steps: Put the point after the first digit, the $5$: $A = 5.84$.
From $58\,400\,000$ to $5.84$, the point moves $7$ places left.
The number is more than $10$, so the power is positive: $n = 7$.
Check: moving the point $7$ places right from $5.84$ gives $58\,400\,000$ again.

blocks.question: Write $0.0006031$ in standard form.
steps: The first non-zero digit is the $6$. Put the point after it: $A = 6.031$.
From $0.0006031$ to $6.031$, the point moves $4$ places right.
The number is less than $1$, so the power is negative: $n = -4$.

blocks.text: Writing $10^{4}$ instead of $10^{-4}$ for a small number. A number less than $1$ always has a negative power.

blocks.hint: Count the places from the current point to just after the $4$.
blocks.explain: The point moves $5$ places right, and the number is less than $1$, so $n = -5$. $41.9 \times 10^{-6}$ has the right value, but $41.9$ is not below $10$.

blocks.text: A working answer such as $73.4 \times 10^{5}$ has the right value but the wrong form. Write $73.4 = 7.34 \times 10^{1}$, then add the powers: $7.34 \times 10^{6}$.

blocks.hint: Write $0.62$ in standard form first, then add the powers.
blocks.explain: $0.62 = 6.2 \times 10^{-1}$, and $-1 + (-3) = -4$. Making $A$ bigger means the power must go down.

blocks.text: To put numbers in standard form in order, compare the powers first. A bigger power means a bigger number. Compare the $A$ values only when the powers are equal.

blocks.hint: Look at the powers of $10$ before the $A$ values.
blocks.explain: $10^{5}$ is the biggest power, so $2.3 \times 10^{5} = 230\,000$ is largest. $9.6$ is the biggest $A$, but $9.6 \times 10^{3}$ is only $9600$.

blocks.text: Core students calculate with standard form only on Paper 3, with a calculator. Extended students also meet it on Paper 2, without one. Working by hand shows what the calculator does.
Use the [[rules-of-indices|rules of indices]]: $10^{a} \times 10^{b} = 10^{a + b}$ and $10^{a} \div 10^{b} = 10^{a - b}$.
1. Multiply (or divide) the $A$ parts. 2. Add (or subtract) the powers. 3. If the new $A$ is less than $1$, or $10$ or more, fix it as in the last section.

blocks.question: Work out $(2.5 \times 10^{7}) \times (8 \times 10^{-3})$. Give your answer in [[standard-form|standard form]].
steps: Multiply the $A$ parts: $2.5 \times 8 = 20$.
Add the powers: $7 + (-3) = 4$. This gives $20 \times 10^{4}$.
$20$ is not less than $10$. Write $20 = 2 \times 10^{1}$, so the answer is $2 \times 10^{1} \times 10^{4} = 2 \times 10^{5}$.

blocks.question: Work out $(1.2 \times 10^{4}) \div (4 \times 10^{-2})$. Give your answer in standard form.
steps: Divide the $A$ parts: $1.2 \div 4 = 0.3$.
Subtract the powers: $4 - (-2) = 6$. This gives $0.3 \times 10^{6}$.
$0.3$ is less than $1$. Write $0.3 = 3 \times 10^{-1}$, so the answer is $3 \times 10^{-1} \times 10^{6} = 3 \times 10^{5}$.

blocks.text: Stopping at $20 \times 10^{4}$. The value is right, but $20$ is not below $10$, so it is not standard form.

blocks.prompt: Work out $(6 \times 10^{5}) \times (7 \times 10^{-9})$. Give your answer in standard form.
Work out $(9 \times 10^{3}) \div (1.5 \times 10^{8})$. Give your answer in standard form.
blocks.explain: $9 \div 1.5 = 6$ and $3 - 8 = -5$, so the answer is $6 \times 10^{-5}$. Adding the powers gives $10^{11}$.

sections.heading: Adding, subtracting and using a calculator

blocks.text: Powers add only when you multiply. To add or subtract by hand, write both numbers as ordinary numbers, work it out, then convert back.

blocks.question: Work out $6.4 \times 10^{5} + 3.8 \times 10^{4}$. Give your answer in [[standard-form|standard form]].
steps: Write both as ordinary numbers: $640\,000$ and $38\,000$.
Convert back: the point moves $5$ places, so $678\,000 = 6.78 \times 10^{5}$.

blocks.text: Adding the $A$ parts when the powers are different. $6.4 + 3.8$ means nothing here: line up the place values first.
On Papers 3 and 4, type standard form with the calculator's power-of-$10$ key. Write down the full display, then round.

blocks.question: A space probe travels at $1.1 \times 10^{4}$ metres per second. How far does it travel in a year of $365$ days? Write the answer in standard form, rounded to $3$ significant figures.
steps: Seconds in the year: $365 \times 24 \times 60 \times 60 = 31\,536\,000$.
Distance $=$ speed $\times$ time $= 1.1 \times 10^{4} \times 31\,536\,000$.
The calculator shows $3.46896 \times 10^{11}$, which is $346\,896\,000\,000$.
Round to $3$ significant figures: $3.47 \times 10^{11}$ m.

blocks.prompt: Work out $5.03 \times 10^{-2} - 7.6 \times 10^{-3}$. Give your answer in standard form.
blocks.hint: Write both as decimals first: $0.0503$ and $0.0076$.
blocks.explain: $0.0503 - 0.0076 = 0.0427 = 4.27 \times 10^{-2}$. Subtracting $7.6$ from $5.03$ ignores the different powers.

blocks.text: Positive number $10$ or more: positive power. From $1$ to under $10$: power $0$. Less than $1$: negative power.
Multiply: multiply the $A$ parts, add the powers. Divide: divide them, subtract the powers. Then fix $A$.
Add or subtract: change to ordinary numbers first.
Compare: biggest power first, then the $A$ values.

mistakes: Leaving $A$ outside $1 \le A < 10$, as in $36 \times 10^{4}$. The value is right but the form is not: write $3.6 \times 10^{5}$.
Getting the sign of the power wrong. A number less than $1$, like $0.007$, has a negative power: $7 \times 10^{-3}$.
Miscounting the places the point moves. Convert your answer back and count the zeros.
Comparing only the $A$ values. $9.1 \times 10^{2}$ is smaller than $1.2 \times 10^{3}$, because the power matters first.
Adding the powers when adding numbers. Powers add only when you multiply.
examTips: “Give your answer in standard form”: an ordinary number, or an $A$ outside $1$ to $10$, can lose the mark even when the value is right.
“Work out” on Paper 3 or 4: write the calculation you type in and the full display, then round to $3$ significant figures unless the question says otherwise.
On Paper 2, show the $A$ parts and the powers on separate lines. Correct working can still earn a mark if the final form slips.
